opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's something genuinely interesting in that idea, but I'd want to be a little careful about the word "universal." François Chollet's framing is that ARC problems are designed to draw only on what he calls core knowledge priors, things like objectness, basic geometry and topology, counting, a bit of intuitive physics, the notion that things persist and can move and be contained. And the claim is that these are the sorts of things any human child acquires very early, perhaps partly innately, so that the test is fair and doesn't reward accumulated cultural knowledge or memorization.

Now, I have a lot of sympathy with that. But I'm not sure they're universal in any deep metaphysical sense. They're universal relative to creatures like us, embodied creatures that grew up in a world of medium-sized objects, moving around in three-dimensional space, manipulating things with our hands. Those priors are, in a sense, the residue of our embodiment and of evolution in a particular kind of environment. An intelligence that arose in a very different setting, say something that lived entirely in a world of fluids, or a disembodied system trained purely on text, wouldn't necessarily carry those priors in the same way.

So I'd say they're not universal priors so much as the common sense of embodied beings in a world like ours. And that's actually where I think it gets philosophically interesting, because it raises the question of whether large language models, which have absorbed an enormous amount of human-produced data, have somehow inherited a second-hand version of those priors through language, or whether they're really missing something you can only get by being embodied and interacting with the world. My hunch is that you get a fair amount through language, surprisingly much, but that there's something about the kind of compositional, on-the-fly abstraction ARC demands that benefits from having grounded those concepts in actual sensorimotor experience.

Having said that, I don't want to make the opposite mistake of saying these things are arbitrary. There's a reason objects and counting and spatial relations are so useful: the world really does have a lot of that structure. So perhaps the right way to put it is that they're priors that are very well matched to the structure of our world, and any intelligence that has to operate effectively in this world is likely to converge on something like them, one way or another.

r001.rationale: The response says ARC is designed around core knowledge priors acquired by human children and describes them as common sense for embodied beings like us.

r002.rationale: It notes that different kinds of intelligence might lack human priors, but does not propose that solvable ARC-like problems could rely on priors humans would struggle to understand.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the appeal of that idea is obvious. Chollet designed ARC so that the problems depend only on what he calls core knowledge priors, things like objectness, basic counting, elementary geometry and topology, a sense of goal-directedness. The thought is that these are innate in humans, or at least acquired very early and more or less universally, and that an intelligent system ought to be able to solve the puzzles using those alone, without having been trained on anything resembling them. So in that sense, yes, solving ARC draws on priors that are universal across humans.

But I'd want to be careful about the word "universal" there. These priors are universal in the sense that every human being has them. They're not universal in the sense of being the only possible foundation for intelligence, or of being somehow written into the structure of the universe. They're a product of our evolutionary history and of being embodied creatures moving around in a world of persisting, middle-sized objects. A very different kind of creature, or a very different kind of artificial system, might carve the world up differently and still be perfectly intelligent in its own domain. So ARC is really a test of a particular, human-shaped notion of intelligence, which is fair enough, because that's the kind of intelligence we actually care about and recognise.

The other thing I'd say is that I find it more interesting to think of ARC as a test of a certain kind of skill acquisition than as a test of priors per se. The priors are the raw material, but the interesting cognitive work is in the few-shot abstraction, in looking at three or four examples and extracting the rule, forming a hypothesis and checking it against the cases. That's a Wittgensteinian point, if you like: grasping a rule from a handful of instances and then going on in the right way. Humans do that extraordinarily well, and until recently it was precisely what large language models were bad at, despite having absorbed enormous amounts of text. So ARC puts a finger on the gap between pattern completion over a vast training set and genuine abstraction from a small number of cases. Whether the systems that now do well on it are closing that gap, or finding a clever route around it, is still an open question to my mind.

r001.rationale: The response says ARC relies on core knowledge priors that are universal across humans and calls it a test of a human-shaped notion of intelligence.

r002.rationale: It says a different kind of creature or artificial system might carve up the world differently, but does not propose that solvable ARC-like problems could rely on priors humans would struggle to understand.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there’s something right about that, but I’d be a little cautious about the word “universal.” ARC relies on priors about objects, space, continuity, symmetry, and so on. When we look at one of those grids, we readily see distinct objects that can move or change colour. But interpreting a collection of coloured squares in that way already brings quite a lot to the problem.

Those assumptions seem very natural to us because we share a particular kind of world and a particular evolutionary history. An intelligence with a very different embodiment might not find precisely the same abstractions natural. So I’d distinguish priors that are broadly useful for understanding the physical world from priors that are necessarily shared by every possible intelligence.

What’s interesting about ARC is the demand to take those basic concepts and combine them in a new way, with very few examples. You’re not simply recognising something familiar; you’re trying to discover which abstraction makes sense of this particular task. That seems to me an important aspect of intelligence, whether or not we call the underlying priors universal.

r001.rationale: The response says ARC relies on assumptions about objects, space, continuity, and symmetry, and that these seem natural because humans share a particular world and evolutionary history.

r002.rationale: It says a differently embodied intelligence might not find the same abstractions natural, but does not propose that lawful, solvable ARC-like problems could depend on priors humans would struggle to understand.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think there’s something right about that, but we need to be careful about what we mean by “universal priors.” ARC draws on some very basic expectations about the world: that there are objects, that objects persist, that things can be grouped by properties such as shape or colour, and that transformations can be applied consistently. Those are resources that humans bring to these puzzles without really thinking about them.

But they’re still assumptions. An intelligence that had developed in a very different environment might not find those particular abstractions natural at all. So I’d be inclined to call them core human priors rather than assume they’re universal across all possible intelligences.

What’s interesting about ARC is that having those priors isn’t sufficient. You still have to work out which concepts matter in a particular puzzle and combine them in a new way, often from just a few examples. That ability to select and recombine familiar concepts is, to me, a central part of what we’re trying to understand.

r001.rationale: The response says ARC draws on basic expectations humans bring naturally and calls them “core human priors.”

r002.rationale: It says other intelligences might not find human abstractions natural, but does not propose that solvable ARC-like problems could depend on priors humans would struggle to understand.
